newsitem.title: USA: S&P assigns "pi" ratings to five Mexican Banks.
newsitem.headline: S&P assigns "pi" ratings to five Mexican Banks.

text.p: Standard & Poor's has assigned public information "pi" ratings to five Mexican banks, all of which fell in the speculative-grade categories of double-B "pi" and single-B "pi."

Among the five banks receiving "pi" ratings, three were rated double-B "pi": Banca Serfin, Banco Internacional, and Banco Mercantil del Norte (Banorte). The remaining two banks, Banco Mexicano and Confia, were rated single-B "pi.".
In comparison, Banco Nacionale de Mexico's (Banamex) local currency counterparty rating is triple-B-minus on S&P's traditional scale.
S&P made the rating assignments on Monday, December 16.
The following summarizes each of the S&P reports.

Confia, established as a retail bank, grew rapidly through an extensive operating infrastructure and an unstable nonretail funding base. Its capitalization ratios weakened as loan growth outstripped capital generation.

With assets equivalent to US$4.19 billion as of Sept 30, 1996, the bank ranks ninth in the Mexican banking system. It faces exceptional challenges to improve its financial condition and its operations to maintain its market position.

Confia recently received two capital infusions from Procapte, the temporary capitalization program provided by Fobaproa to maintain solvency ratios at minimum regulatory levels. Confia's parent, Abaco Grupo Financiero, presently is negotiating a capital injection from the Principal Group, of Des Moines, Iowa.

If successfully concluded, the transaction will bolster Confia's equity position and stabilize its financial condition. Confia has sold over 20 percent of its loans to the government in two separate transactions. The bank required liquidity support from the government in 1995.
Banco Internacional is the fifth largest Mexican bank in terms of loans and deposits as of Sept 30, 1996.

Standard & Poor's believes Banco Internacional is the strongest domestic bank in Mexico after Banamex and Bancomer. During the past three years, the bank has repositioned itself by expanding and modernizing its branch network in Mexico's major business centers, moving away from its previous focus on financing public expenditures and being subject to rigid government control.

Asset quality deteriorated sharply as a result of the rapid increase in interest rates in the wake of the peso devaluation, and problems were exacerbated by the bank's loan concentration in retail and middle-market segments, the segments most affected by the crisis.

Based on data provided earlier in the year, the bank's non-performing loans under present reporting standards dropped to 4.8 percent of total loans, reflecting the sale of bad loans to the government in two operations, representing 20 percent of its loan portfolio.
The bank made limited use of the liquidity facility provided by the government in early 1995.

Banorte's asset quality measures are somewhat better than those of other banks in the system, partially due to two loan sales to the government for approximately 14 percent of total loans. Banorte's financial profile is hurt by its recent rapid growth, which has outstripped its deposit base, and by its support of the troubled Bancentro.
S&P is also concerned about Banorte's publicly stated aggressive acquisition strategy.
Banco Mexicano's weak capital ratios and low profitability prevent it from benefitting from its position as the fourth-largest bank in the system.

The bank, with assets totaling US$11.3 billion as of Sept 30, 1996, already had a fragile financial profile when the peso devaluation occurred. This profile resulted from its strategy of emphasizing aggressive corporate loan growth funded by wholesale deposits and interbank loans, all at the expense of profitability and capital generation.

Mexicano accessed the liquidity facilties provided by the government in early 1995. In October 1996, Banco Santander signed a letter of intent to acquire eventually up to 75 percent of Banco Mexicano's holding company.

The operation includes additional sales of bad loans and underperforming assets to the government, bringing the total to approximately US$3.5 billion. The "pi" rating on Banco Mexicano may be upgraded once Santander converts the subordinated convertible debt into capital.
Banca Serfin, with 13 percent of the market, is Mexico's third-largest bank as of Sept 30, 1996.

Most of its loan growth in recent years has been funded through high-cost purchased funds, leaving the bank with weak net interest income. While the bank has implemented strategies to attract more customer deposits, it must contend with fierce competition from stronger institutions.
S&P believes that Serfin remains critical to the Mexican banking system and will continue to receive support if needed. Its "pi" rating partly reflects this priveledged position.
Serfin has sold one-third of its loan portfolio to the government and accessed the liquidity facilities offered by authorities in 1995.

The public information rating criteria for financial institutions notes that it is in line with S&P's rating practices in the United States corporate and global insurance markets. Further, the public information rating criteria parallels the analytical methodology S&P applies in its traditional ratings, but does not rely on receiving ongoing access to management.
Launched earlier this year, BankRatings Service is being expanded to accommodate the addition of approximately 250 new public information bank ratings, predominantly in emerging markets, S&P said.
